title: Constructive Greedy Approach for Forbidden Integer
approach_explanation: The problem asks whether we can sum numbers from 1 to k, excluding x, to reach n. If x != 1, we can simply use 1 exclusively, since 1 is not forbidden. If x == 1, we cannot use 1. If k == 1, no numbers are available, so the answer is NO. If k >= 2 and n is even, we can use n/2 twos. If n is odd and k >= 3, we can use a single 3 and (n - 3) / 2 twos. If n is odd and k == 2, it is impossible since we only have 2 available and cannot form an odd sum.

code_breakdown.explanation: Read the number of test cases `t` and loop through each test case parsing `n`, `k`, and `x`.
If `x` is not 1, 1 is available. We can trivially form any sum `n` using `n` ones. Output YES, `n`, followed by `n` ones.
If `x == 1` and `k == 1`, no valid integers remain in the range [1, k] except 1, which is forbidden. Thus, output NO.

code_breakdown.section_title: Case 3: x == 1 and n is even
code_breakdown.explanation: If `n` is even and `x == 1`, we can form `n` using `n / 2` copies of the integer 2.

code_breakdown.section_title: Case 4: x == 1 and n is odd
code_breakdown.explanation: If `n` is odd and `x == 1`, we check `k`. If `k == 2`, it's impossible because we can only use 2s to form an even sum. If `k >= 3`, we can use one 3 and `(n - 3) / 2` twos.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each testcase, the solution constructs and prints the answer using at most $N$ elements. Across $t$ testcases, the total time is proportional to the sum of $N$, which is bounded by $t 	imes N \≤ 100 	imes 100 = 10^4$ operations, well within the 2-second time limit.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: The solution only uses a few scalar variables for input and loops, directly streaming the output without allocating auxiliary arrays or containers.

strengths: Handles all edge cases systematically (e.g., k=1, x=1, odd/even n).
Direct stream outputs keep memory consumption constant at $O(1)$.
Clean branching structure reflecting case analysis.
edge_cases_handled: n is odd with x=1 and k=2 (impossible case handled correctly).
k=1 with x=1 (no elements available handled correctly).
n is even with x=1 (handled with twos).
best_practices_feedback: Prefer `\n` instead of `endl` for competitive programming to prevent performance slowdowns due to stream flushing.
Consider fast I/O (`ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(NULL);`) for larger constraints.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Adding `cin.tie(NULL)` speeds up standard input/output streams significantly for large test cases.
